hero.headline: St. Lucie schools superintendent pledges review after bus flooding incident
hero.teaser: St. Lucie school superintendent Jon Prince pledges to review district decisions during the Nov. 2 flooding after a student waded through chest-high water.cisions during the Nov. 2
hero.body:
St. Lucie Public Schools Superintendent Dr. Jon Prince said the district will review its policies and decisions during the Nov. 2 flooding after video showed a student wading through chest-high water after getting off a school bus in Port St. Lucie. Prince said officials are examining whether the district could have responded differently.

 The review pledge comes as district schools and offices remain closed Wednesday, Nov. 18, amid another flood threat. Prince said officials would monitor conditions and decide late Wednesday afternoon whether to cancel Thursday classes. He said he hoped the precaution would prove unnecessary but did not want to risk another dangerous situation. “The ground is so saturated, but if the conditions worsen tomorrow, we don't want a repeat of what happened November 2,” Prince said.

 The video from Nov. 2 shows the boy stepping off a school bus on SW Coleman Avenue and walking through floodwaters that reach as high as his chest. Critics have pointed to the video in questioning the district’s actions. Prince apologized Tuesday night for the stress families experienced. “It was very stressful for our families, and I certainly apologize for the stress that they went through on that day,” he said.

 Prince said the flooding was unexpected and that decisions were based on information available at the time. He said every decision made that day is being analyzed. “We are going to review all our procedures, our policies to make sure that if there's anything that we could have done differently, that moving forward we will,” he said.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County estimates $60 million shortfall as crews prepare for flooding threat
cards.teaser: The preliminary estimate reflects Amendment 3’s additional homestead exemption. County crews are deploying again after storm work two weeks ago generated unbudgeted overtime.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County is estimating a $60 million revenue shortfall next fiscal year under Amendment 3, which increases the homestead exemption, as crews deploy for another threat of rain and flooding. County spokesman Erick Gill said the preliminary estimate comes as county leaders consider their budgets and the costs of storm preparation and response.

 Gill said the estimated shortfall would grow to about $120 million once the exemption increases further. “We're looking at the early estimates in this next upcoming fiscal year to be about a $60 million shortfall and then about $120 million once the exemption goes up.”

 Crews are being deployed across the county as they were two weeks ago, Gill said. He estimated that 50 to 100 staff members, including public works crews, worked in the field during that storm, generating unbudgeted overtime. “I think everybody is well aware now that this storm drain system was not designed for the flooding we're getting nowadays,” Gill said.

 This week, the county offered residents free sand to bag as another round of November rain and flooding threatened Florida's east coast. Dickerson Infrastructure and Stewart Materials donated the sand. Gill said other services cost money, with the coming Amendment 3 tax cuts already on county leaders’ minds.
